resolved_by: Mathis v. United States, 136 S. Ct. 2243 (2016) (Supreme Court) resolved the split by holding that a statute listing alternative means of satisfying one element is indivisible, so the modified categorical approach does not apply.
issue: Under the ACCA categorical approach, does a statute that lists alternative means of satisfying a single element become divisible, allowing courts to apply the modified categorical approach?

sides.position: A statute that lists various means of satisfying one element is still indivisible; the modified categorical approach applies only to statutes with alternative elements.
cases: United States v. Cabrera-Umanzor, 728 F.3d 347 (4th Cir. 2013)

sides.position: The general rule that a crime counts as a predicate only if its elements match the generic offense gives way when a statute lists various means of satisfying an element, so the modified categorical approach applies.

this_court: Adopts the view that alternative means do not make a statute divisible, consistent with Mathis and Omargharib; the opinion describes the contrary position as an exception it rejects.
quote: the Court set forth the circuit split that developed, in which some courts held that “ACCA’s general rule -- that a defendant’s crime of conviction can count as a predicate only if its elements match those of a generic offense -- gives way when a statute happens to list various means by which a defendant can satisfy an element.”
cite: John Ham, Jr. v. Warden M. Breckon, 994 F.3d 682 (4th Cir. 2021)
